GOKMEN TEACHING
Computational Practice
Computational Design Seminar
*The course was taught across Spring 2025  (64 stu-
dents) and Spring 2026 (80 students), with the struc-
ture evolving through repeated delivery and expanded 
support from teaching assistants.
Course Summary 
Computational Practice introduced students to 
contemporary methods in computational design 
through the combined study of parametric modeling, 
geometry, materiality, and digital fabrication. As part 
of the computational design curriculum, the course 
advanced students from foundational parametric con-
cepts toward architectural applications that connect 
digital workflows with physical production. 
 
The seminar followed a dual trajectory: paramet-
ric façades and minimal surfaces. These two topics 
allowed students to explore computation at different 
scales and through different mediums. The façade 
module focused on precedent analysis, parametric 
modeling, and geometric variation. The minimal 
surface module shifted toward form-finding, topolo-
gy, mesh modeling, physics-based simulation, digital 
fabrication, and installation-scale assembly. T ogether, 
the course positioned computational practice as both 
a technical discipline and a design methodology. 
 
The course emphasized that computational tools 
are most valuable when they support design rigor. 
Students were asked to move beyond software execu-
tion and toward an understanding of how geometric 
systems are structured, controlled, varied, fabricated, 
and evaluated. Assignments introduced progressively 
complex workflows, helping students develop con-
fidence in Rhinoceros, Grasshopper, and associated 
plug-ins while connecting digital models to architec-
tural problems. 
 
Methodology 
The semester was organized around twelve weekly 
exercises and two major group projects for a large 
cohort of students. Each exercise introduced a specific 
computational workflow, gradually building student 
competency in computational tools and workflows. 
This scaffolded structure allowed students to build flu-
ency through repetition while applying each new skill 
to a larger project sequence. 
 
The course operated as an open workshop environ-
ment. Approximately thirty percent of class time was 
dedicated to lectures, demonstrations, and concep-
tual introductions, while seventy percent was work-
shop-based. Students followed online tutorials pre-
pared by the instructor, worked through template files 
and scripts, and received technical support from the 
instructor and teaching assistants during class. This 
format allowed students to proceed at different speeds, 
revisit material independently, and develop practical 
skills through guided experimentation. 
 
Course Structure 
The semester was divided into three instructional 
sequences: Parametric Façades, Generative AI W ork-
shop, and Minimal Surfaces. 
 
Module I: Parametric Façades 
The first module introduced students to parametric 
façade systems through precedent analysis and gen-
erative modeling. W orking in pairs, students selected 
contemporary façade precedents and developed scripts 
capable of reproducing and varying their geometric 
systems. W eekly workshops introduced NURBS mod-
eling, graph structures, logic operators, subdivision, 
panelization, and façade system development. The fi-
nal outcome included a scaled model of the precedent 
façade and a series of parametric variations. 
 
This module asked students to understand façades 
as systems of rules, subdivisions, panels, and variable 
geometric relationships. Through this process, stu-
dents learned how computational tools can be used 
to analyze architectural precedents and translate them 
into operational design systems. 
 
Module II: AI W orkshop 
A one-day AI workshop introduced students to Stable 
Diffusion workflows for architectural visualization. 
Students used AI-assisted rendering as a representa-
tional extension of their parametric work, testing how 
image-generation tools could support visual explora-
tion, atmosphere, and communication. This module 
connected computational modeling to emerging 
visualization techniques and helped students situate 
AI within a broader design workflow. 
 
Module III: Minimal Surfaces 
The second major project focused on minimal sur-
faces, form-finding, and digital fabrication. W orking 
in groups of three or four, students developed topo-
logical models that could be rationalized, segmented, 
fabricated, and assembled as installation-scale projects. 
W orkshops introduced mesh modeling, W eaverbird, 
Kangaroo physics, mesh segmentation, joinery, and 
fabrication workflows. 
 
This module emphasized the relationship between 
geometry and material assembly. Students translat-
ed abstract computational forms into constructible 
systems, developing protocols for fabrication, jointing, 
segmentation, and physical construction. The final 
work demonstrated how computational geometry 
can move from screen-based exploration into material 
practice. 
 
Student W ork Presented 
The student work from this course documents a pro-
gression from precedent-based parametric modeling to 
digitally fabricated minimal surface installations. Proj-
ects include façade analyses, parametric variation ma-
trices, AI-assisted renderings, mesh-based form-finding 
studies, fabrication diagrams, joinery systems, mock-
ups, and installation-scale assemblies. 
 
Learning Outcomes 
Students developed technical proficiency in Rhi-
noceros, Grasshopper, and computational modeling 
workflows while strengthening their ability to think 
through geometry, topology, variation, and fabrica-
tion. They learned to analyze architectural precedents 
as parametric systems, construct scripts that produce 
controlled design variations, translate digital geom-
etry into physical models, and collaborate on fabri-
cation-based projects. The course reinforced com-
putational design as a process-oriented practice that 
connects research, experimentation, representation, 
materiality, and making.
UNC Charlotte School of Architecture

We began by generating elliptical profiles in Grasshopper
and experimenting with multiplication and rotated copies,
stacking each ellipse vertically while rotating it at twice
the angle of the profile below to produce a continuous
twisting motion. These layered curves were lofted to
establish the initial tower form, allowing us to study
rotational geometry before refining the mass through
SubD modeling. From this sculpted volume, we derived
floor-by-floor sections to generate parametric slabs and
continuous balcony rings, translating abstract geometry
into inhabitable space. Balcony edge curves then became
the driving logic for the railing system, where evenly
spaced vertical posts and continuous handrails were
developed as a modular component, enabling the façade,
balconies, and circulation elements to respond
dynamically as a unified parametric system.

Before transitioning into SubD, we began by generating stacked elliptical profiles in Grasshopper, rotating each curve at twice
the angle of the one below to produce a spiraling vertical system. These curves were lofted to establish the primary tower
mass, allowing us to explore rotational continuity through NURBS geometry, while a separate control script enabled us to
manipulate the entire form through a single parameter slider. From this lifted spiral, we extracted guiding lines that informed
our curtain wall system, using this logic to organize façade panel placement and vertical rhythm. The mullions were thickened
using the Pipe command to establish structural hierarchy, emphasizing primary vertical elements while allowing secondary
members to remain lighter and more transparent.

import Rhino.Geometry as rg
import math
# Initialize the output list
FlowerCurves = []
# Loop through every hole plane you generated
for plane in Planes:
    points = []
    num_samples = 100 # Controls how smooth the curve is
    
    for i in range(num_samples):
        # Calculate the angle in radians
        t = (i / float(num_samples)) * 2 * math.pi
        
        # The polar math magic for the flower shape
        r = BaseRadius + Amplitude * math.cos(Petals * t)
        
        # Convert polar back to Cartesian (X, Y)
        x = r * math.cos(t)
        y = r * math.sin(t)
        
        # Map the 2D flower onto your 3D panel's plane
        pt = plane.PointAt(x, y)
        points.append(pt)
        
    # Add the very first point to the end to perfectly close the shape
    points.append(points[0])
    
    # Generate a smooth NURBS curve from the points
    curve = rg.Curve.CreateInterpolatedCurve(points, 3)
    FlowerCurves.append(curve)

LOBBY AND PENTHOUSE
CURTAIN WALL
ROOF TO END CURTAIN WALL 
We began by referencing an elliptical curve that defines the
perimeter of the mechanical penthouse enclosure at the top of
the tower. Using a series of vertical translations in the Z
direction, the ellipse was duplicated and stacked at consistent
heights to establish the horizontal glass bands, which were then
lofted to create the continuous glazed enclosure. To articulate
the façade system, the base ellipse was divided into evenly
spaced points that generate vertical mullion lines extending the
full height of the enclosure. These lines were then piped to
produce the structural mullion elements, creating a parametric
glass room whose height, band spacing, and mullion density
can all be adjusted through slider parameters.

Mediopadana Station | Santiago Calatrava
Reggio Emilia, Italy 2013
Located in Reggio Emilia, Italy the Mediopadana station designed by the 
famous Santiago Calatrava creates a beautiful skeletal-like structure. The 
building primarily compromises its enveloped facade, encapsulating the 
station from front to back. The form resembles waves with both vertical 
and horizontal directionality. The top canopy is aligned with glass that 
runs along the steel waves making it look like there is only the skeletal 
structure above. Lastly, the structure itself uses 25 steel ports and reaches 
a total distance of 483 meters.

of these 3 middle cells features a 
cylindrical span that connects the

geometry is shown on the left. Once

“Scherk with Handle” Variations
Form-Finding
Using the original Scherk-with-handle geometry, 
the base formwork was mirrored vertically and left 
untrimmed in its natural checkerboard pattern.
The original formwork is flipped onto its side and 
mirrored along the x-axis. The resulting geometry 
generates large circular openings, with two small 
holes positioned next to each other that pierce the 
full length.
The untrimmed version of the Scherk with handle 
features altered proportions to make the side 
“wings” smaller. The center point of these was also 
lowered below the midpoint.

SCHOEN’S BA TWING SURFACE
Minimal Surface Study | Topology + Symmetry
Definition
Schoen’s batwing surface is a minimal surface derived from the study of triply periodic 
minimal surfaces. It is defined by zero mean curvature and constructed through symmetry 
operations that generate a continuous, non-self-intersecting structure.
Key Properties
-Zero mean curvature (minimal surface)
-Derived from TPMS framework
-High genus (multiple openings)
-Continuous surface (no edges or boundaries)
Symmetry + Topology
The surface is generated from a fundamental region using mirror and rotational 
symmetry. A C2 symmetry axis (180° rotation) allows the formation of paired regions, 
producing the characteristic “batwing” geometry. Repetition of these regions 
constructs a cubic unit cell and larger periodic lattice.
Topologically, the surface is continuous and high genus, forming an interconnected 
network of voids without boundaries or self-intersections.

LASERCUT SHEETS
Lasercut on 18"x24" Bristol paper, 
the 96 strips consist of five unique 
sheets repeated to account for 
the symmetry of our minimal 
surface. The final physical model is 
assembled as a 3x3x3 structure.
The strips are connected through  
tabs that create a flush edge and 
are secured with split pins. This 
technique emphasizes the 
surface's topology, revealing the 
specific transitions where the 
minimal surface flips inside out.

Triangulated Neovius Surface
Surface formulation with Equation
The iteration demonstrates how manipulating the domain parameter of the implicit surface 
equation controls the periodicity, density, and morphology of the Schwartz P TPMS. As the 
domain expands, the surface tiles across space producing multiple unit cells. As the domain 
contracts or shifts, the surface transitions from an open lattice to a closed, solid-dominant 
geometry with reduced porosity.The surface also flipped throughout the process.
